Honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. They've got all the delicious elements of pie—flaky, buttery crust and tender baked fruit—but none of the fussy technique. With galettes, you don’t have to worry about any crimping, latticework, or blind baking. Sometimes, it's okay to take the easy road. This classic apple galette is one of our favorite examples. Warm, comforting, and bursting with sweet, spiced flavor, it’s everything you love about apple pie with a fraction of the effort.

What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice. Really really nice recipe. So fast and simple, not too sweet and not at all goopy. This will be my go-to filling for apple galettes from now on.” - PurpleRing.

According to recent reports, first, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl. Then, preheat the oven to 400° and prepare a baking sheet by lining it with parchment paper. Coat a clean surface with a dusting of flour, then roll the chilled pie dough into a 12” circle that is about ⅛” thick. Transfer the dough to the baking sheet.

It has been revealed that arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

Recent findings suggest that brush the egg wash over the crust and sprinkle demerara sugar over the top. Then place the galette into the oven to bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is fragrant and tender. Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

Anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

You need, expectedly, Original capsules for Original machines and Vertuo capsules for Vertuo machines. I've broken down the differences between the lines below, and the defining details about specific models in each line that are on sale right now. And be sure to bookmark this story because we’ll enhancement it with more Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on Nespresso coffee makers and espresso machines as they happen.

Sources indicate that introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. Some Vertuo machines can even fill an 18-ounce carafe from a single coffee pod.

The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

Enabled with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, the Nespresso Vertuo Next can brew 18 ounces of coffee from a single pod. If you’re intrigued by the tech or pod yield, it’s worth a try—especially considering Nespresso’s 30-day return policy, warranty, and reputation for maintenance and machine repairs.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

This compact machine heats up in just three seconds (which, is really, really, ridiculously fast for any coffee maker to heat water) and depending on the specific model you get, it can brew six or seven different cup sizes, ranging from a single shot of espresso to a full carafe from a single Vertuo pod. Like the Next and Pop machines, the Vertuo Up is Wi-Fi enabled and you can use the companion app for maintenance alerts and to customize how the machine brews your favorite pods, if you'd like tweaks to the pod-specific presets.

The Vertuo Creatista is the first machine in the Vertuo line with a built-in steam wand. It’s not quite a one-touch cappuccino machine because brewing espresso from a pod and steaming the milk are two separate processes. But if you want the look of a real espresso machine (well, if you don’t look too closely) with the convenience of Nespresso Vertuo capsules, the Vertuo Creatista is a great option. This is the machine that I’ve been using at home for years and it works sort of like a super-automatic espresso machine.

The newest Vertuo machine, the Vertuo Lattissima is a one-touch machine that makes coffee, espresso, cappuccinos, and latte macchiatos at the push of a button.

Until the Vertuoline was introduced in 2014, the OriginalLine machines were simply known as Nespresso machines. These models brew either single or lungo (Italian for "long") espresso-style shots from any compatible pod using a pressure-driven method. The Original Line features a collection of compact pod-only machines (Nespresso CitiZ, Nespresso Essenza Mini, and Nespresso Pixie) as well as a variety of pricier Creatista and Lattissima models, with built-in steam wands or other automatic milk frothers. We rarely see the compact Original machines go on sale, but here are the Nespresso Original Line models you can find for a steal ahead of Black Friday.

According to recent reports, even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from noted anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

It has been revealed that cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

According to recent reports, I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

Industry observers note that according to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Sources indicate that moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Industry observers note that of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

Industry observers note that for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

In a recent development, this is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

And if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

The cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

The combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That said, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

The crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

The gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Industry observers note that storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

In a recent development, never in your life have you had such an exemplary vegetable as these boiled potatoes, inspired by the version featured in the 2005 film adaptation of Pride and Prejudice. While the moment is not part of Jane Austen’s classic novel, the simple dish has developed a bit of a cult following. Our interpretation has a little garlic and lemon zest in addition to plenty of butter and parsley; we think Mr. Collins would approve—dare we say, he may even declare them excellent. Don your finest Regency-style garb and place a pot of water on the hearth: We have potatoes to boil.

Even more excellent potato recipes this way.

Combine ¼ cup Diamond Crystal or 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Morton kosher salt and 10 cups water in a large pot.

In a recent development, peel 1½ lb. Yukon Gold potatoes (about 3 large or 4 medium). Quarter if potatoes are large, halve if medium, adding to pot as you go. Potatoes should be covered by at least 2" water when finished; add more if needed.

In a recent development, place pot over high heat and bring water to a boil. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer until potatoes are cooked through (a fork should slide easily into flesh), 15–20 minutes. Drain in a colander.

Set pot over medium-low heat to cook off any excess water, then add 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter and cook until melted. Stir in 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper. Remove from heat; mix in ¼ cup finely chopped parsley and 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest. Add drained potatoes and toss to coat. Taste and season with more salt if needed. Transfer potatoes to a large shallow bowl to serve.

Industry News: Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • Industry observers note that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 matter of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Industry observers note that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

It has been revealed that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

It has been revealed that to build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights manufacturer HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

In a recent development, we’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Industry observers note that culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

After a quick boil, each ball is rolled in shredded fresh coconut for a soft, snowy finish.

#112434. Why Is Everyone So Obsessed With Protein?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1895 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Why Is Everyone So Obsessed With Protein?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies.
  • I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands.
  • It has been revealed that in my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies. Whether you’re curious about mindful eating or want to understand what makes picky eaters picky, read on and let award-winning journalist Betsy Andrews answer all your burning questions.

I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands. Carbs make you feel full, at least temporarily, and without them, especially when I’m hungry after a workout, I’m turning to an even more filling macronutrient: protein. I’m 63, and my wife is 60. We’ve heard that dietary protein is key to wellness in aging. But, after recent blood work, she is worrying about “bad,” or LDL, cholesterol. All this leaves me pondering the types and amounts of proteins I should be cooking that won’t increase her cholesterol levels or my waistline but will make for satisfying, healthy meals.

It has been revealed that in my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone. Americans are bingeing on the stuff: Social media is glutted with influencers promoting protein powders and heavy meat consumption; supermarket shelves have filled with packaged snacks advertising excess protein; and restaurants are overhauling menus to feed the needs of protein-hungry diners. Even the latest USDA dietary guidelines encourage protein uptake. At its extreme, it’s a trend known as protein-maxxing, and everyone from the Kardashians to the American Medical Association is talking about it.

Our bodies need protein to function. “Protein is made of amino acids. When we digest protein, we release those amino acids and use them to build and maintain our own proteins: muscle, liver, heart, lungs, and even some bone,” explains kinesiology professor Stuart Phillips, director of the Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE) at Ontario’s McMaster University in Canada. “Protein supplies materials for enzymes, antibodies, transport proteins, some hormones, and the repair of tissues and organs.”.

According to recent reports, of the 20 amino acids in our bodies, nine are essential, meaning we can’t create them ourselves. We must get them from eating protein, and we need to keep up protein consumption, because our bodies deplete it as we digest it. “The simple takeaway is that protein builds you from the inside out. It is foundational,” notes dietitian Daphene Altema-Johnson, senior program officer at the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. “But unlike fat, your body doesn’t have a dedicated storage system for protein, so you need a steady supply from food.”.

In a culture built on body image, protein is also touted for its body-sculpting and weight-loss benefits. “You use protein to help build and maintain muscle mass and also recover from a workout,” explains Zach Rocheleau, the creator of the protein-rich recipes that comprise The Flexible Dieting Lifestyle. “It’s also the most satiating macronutrient. Getting the satiety effects of protein and thus feeling full, so eating less calories, is the driver that goes into losing weight.”.

When influencers like Rocheleau claim that the protein they’re eating has helped them shape their physique, they aren’t wrong. Research does show that if you eat more protein it assists (to a point) in building lean muscle mass during resistance training. And studies have established the relationship between protein consumption, satiation, and weight loss. “The hype has come from real physiological needs,” claims Dr. Megan Rossi, founder of The Gut Health Doctor, “but it’s more of an aesthetic effect, where people associate protein with substantial muscles and think the more protein they eat, the bulkier they’ll get.”.

Scarfing down cheeseburgers and looking great doing it sounds good, but eating too much protein can put stress on your body, especially the kidneys. When you eat protein, Altema-Johnson explains, “The nitrogen part of it is stripped off and converted to urea, which is filtered out by your kidneys. Lots of nitrogen waste leads to a chronically higher kidney workload.”.

For most people, this shouldn’t be much to worry about: Though he notes that this isn’t an endorsement of long-term protein bingeing, Phillips’ meta-analysis found no negative effect of higher protein consumption on kidney function in healthy adults. But if your kidneys aren’t in tip-top shape, stressing them can contribute to high blood pressure and other heart conditions. And studies show that consume excess animal-based proteins, in particular, can increase the risk of kidney stones.

There’s another potential problem: Your small intestine can only digest so much protein, so in high amounts, some of it ends up in your colon, where it can produce potentially harmful by-products. “Excess protein, like poorly absorbed egg whites and red meat, can ferment and produce toxic metabolites, which are associated with heart disease,” indicates Rossi. The solution is to eat fiber as well. But when you’re protein-maxxing, other nutrients, including fiber, can fall to the wayside.

Finally, though protein-maxxing is often touted as a way to slim down, the opposite can be true, too. “Your body has a ceiling for how much protein you can use,” indicates Altema-Johnson. Excess protein gets converted into glucose or fat for energy. Calories are energy units. You only need so many of them, and if you’re “chasing a protein number instead of eating until full,” as Altema-Johnson puts it, studies show that the extra calories can lead to weight gain.

Some protein-enriched packaged foods harbor sneaky calories. According to Rocheleau—who, by the way, eschews the phrase “protein-maxxing” in his work—“You would think that somebody putting out a high-protein product would take calories from carbs and fats and replace them with protein, but generally they keep the product the same but add protein, so you’re getting a lot more calories.” Plus, the marketing of protein-added snacks actually creates an insidious halo effect. “If you slap ‘high protein’ on a package, there’s the perception that it is automatically healthy, which can lead to overconsumption,” says Altema-Johnson. And while dairy- or plant-based protein products, including powdered supplements, can be a convenient way to support higher training needs to fill a genuine gap in the diet, Phillips’ research highlights that they’re not a substitute for exercise itself and that protein intake had diminishing gains over a certain amount.

Recent findings suggest that so what is the optimum amount of protein we should consume? Guidelines differ. Like the USDA previously, Canadian guidelines suggest a daily protein intake of .8 grams per kilogram of body weight. (To convert your body weight from pounds to kilograms, just divide it by 2.2.) For me, at 77 kilograms, 62 grams of protein per day is a good target, according to these guidelines, which comes out to a little over 8 ounces of roast chicken to meet my goals for the day. U.K. guidelines recommend slightly less, at .75 grams per kilogram, while the fresh USDA guidelines have been cranked up to 1.2 to 1.6 grams. At that serving goal, I can scarf down more than a pound of roast bird a day, and in theory, that’s what experts want me to do. For active and older adults, Phillips likes the new USDA targets, because we lose muscle mass as we age, and we start to need more protein to help retain it.

It has been revealed that but not all protein is created equal. With my partner’s concern over cholesterol, maybe a skin-on bird dripping fat or a well-marbled steak seared in butter, both high in saturated fat, isn’t optimal for us. “This is where individualization matters,” claims Altema-Johnson. “The goal is not zero red meat, but smaller proportions, moderation, and smarter cuts.” Experts like her, and plenty of studies, will warn you away from fattier and, especially, processed meats. “Unprocessed steak, ground beef, even pork chops have a modest health-associated risk,” Altema-Johnson says. “But bacon, sausage, deli meat, hot dogs—if you’re eating those constantly, you’re at higher risk for heart disease, colorectal cancer, and other health challenges.”.

Unlike animal proteins, not all plants contain every amino acid that our bodies need. But you can combine various vegetable proteins to meet those goals. Phillips and his colleagues found that young vegan and omnivorous men eating around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day achieved similar muscle and strength gains with resistance training. “Grains tend to be relatively low in lysine. Legumes help address that limitation, while grains complement legumes’ amino acid profiles,” he states. “Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, edamame, eggs, milk, yogurt, nuts, and seeds can all contribute. Soy is a particularly useful plant protein.” You don’t have to mix and match them at every meal, but a diverse plant-based diet can bring the protein you need.

In a recent development, the biggest takeaway is that you can’t just protein-max in the absence of overall healthy lifestyle choices. One of those is a balanced diet. According to Altema-Johnson, we should “individualize, moderate and balance. It’s key to have a diverse plate. If you’re focusing on one type of protein, especially meat, you’re missing out on all the good yummies a body needs.”.

Chief among those yummies is fiber. Rossi claims that recent studies support the idea that increasing protein can have benefits for weight-lifting and even aging, “but you need to increase fiber to balance it so your microbiome has more to eat than just excess protein. We need to swing the fiber flag.” Another recent study showed that 93 percent of Americans get enough protein, but other research reveals the opposite for fiber: Just 7 percent of us eat an adequate amount. That’s not good. A review of more than 5,000 studies found that a diet low in red meat but high in fiber-rich whole grains, vegetables, and nuts lowered our risk of death due to heart disease. “For gut health,” Phillips says, we should “ask what your protein habit is pushing off the plate.”.

The other important lifestyle choice is exercise. “You can’t just expect to be sitting on the couch and eating protein and having these huge gains. Physical activity and resistance training bring far bigger results,” Rossi notes. That’s why I’ve ultimately been committed to moving more: Preventing muscle loss is insurance for my future. “Without enough protein and—most importantly, in my opinion—resistance exercise, this loss speeds up significantly,” says Altema-Johnson. “It affects strength, ability, balance, and fall risk. Muscle loss is directly tied to independence. It’s the difference between carrying your own groceries at 80 or needing help.”.

Of course, I’m getting a late start. “You do not wake up at 65 with a latest protein requirement. Start paying attention in midlife (over 40), and pair the protein with strength training, as that is the significant lever to promote health, not protein,” notes Phillips. Well, I’m not 65 yet, but I did almost hit that age without addressing these health needs. Now I know that I need to exercise, and to support the training, I need a bit more protein, but not piles of it, and it has to come from a variety of sources. Perhaps most importantly, I’ll continue to take whatever the trend-setters are pushing on the socials with a grain of salt. As Phillips puts it, “Protein is a nutrient, not an identity. The goal is enough to support health, not as much as you can eat.”.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

In a recent development, as much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

Sources indicate that I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

Sources indicate that I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

In a recent development, thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

It has been revealed that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host states dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

Industry observers note that I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a massive breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

It has been revealed that I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

Recent findings suggest that first, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a substantial deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

Industry observers note that this is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really crucial to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

It has been revealed that and I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really key for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Industry observers note that it’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

Recent findings suggest that like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

More tasty chicken thigh recipes here.

Sources indicate that toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

It has been revealed that in a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

In a recent development, in a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

Add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

Latest Update: Earth’s Soil Is Worth $325 Trillion – so Why Is Nobody Protecting It?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.
  • It has been revealed that nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface.
  • Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.

It has been revealed that nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface. This vital resource also filters water, stores carbon, and supports ecosystems that sustain life. Yet despite its importance, soil remains without a dedicated international treaty to protect it.

Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.

Binding international agreements protect the atmosphere, biodiversity, and the high seas. Soil, an estimated US$325 trillion (A$473 trillion) natural asset, receives fragmented protection through agreements on climate change, biodiversity, and desertification.

The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification focuses on drylands, while other agreements address individual functions such as carbon storage or biodiversity. None provides comprehensive, binding protection for soil as a planetary system.

The paper’s authors, University of Sydney soil scientists Dr. Quentin Styc and Professor Alex McBratney, argue that this gap partly reflects a misunderstanding of the resource itself.

“We have spent centuries classifying soils according to their different properties, uses and locations. But in doing so, we’ve lost sight of the bigger picture,” stated lead author Dr. Styc, from the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Sydney Institute of Agriculture.

Sources indicate that consider the connection between the Sahara Desert and the Amazon rainforest. Each year, around 27.7 million metric tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, delivering roughly 22,000 metric tons of phosphorus to the Amazon. This natural fertilization replaces nutrients lost through flooding, helping sustain one of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems.

Erosion, pesticide contamination, and microplastics can also spread across borders, while soil degradation can contribute to climate change and food insecurity far from the affected region.

“Soil doesn’t stop functioning at national borders. What happens to soil in one country can have profound consequences for ecosystems, economies and food security on the other side of the world.

“We have international treaties to protect the ocean and atmosphere. Yet the soil beneath our feet, which is fundamental to human civilization, remains without equivalent protection.”.

For Styc and McBratney, these links mean soil must be understood and protected as one interconnected global system.

Recent findings suggest that “These connections demonstrate why soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently,” Dr. Styc noted.

Sources indicate that “We need to think about soil in the singular, just as we increasingly talk about one ocean rather than separate oceans. It’s a change in language that reflects a much bigger change in how we understand our responsibility for the planet.”.

It has been revealed that A proposal for international protection is already taking shape. Aroura, a global soil security think tank established at the University of Sydney, has outlined an eight-stage pathway toward a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The proposed convention would coordinate international efforts while allowing countries to develop strategies suited to their environmental and economic circumstances.

In October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature approved a resolution calling for a binding international legal instrument on soil security. Ocean governance offers a model for what cooperation could achieve. After decades of negotiations, an international agreement protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdictions entered into force in January 2026.

Recent findings suggest that “When environmental damage crosses borders, international cooperation needs to match the scale of the problem. We cannot solve a planetary challenge with a patchwork of disconnected policies,” Dr. Styc said.

It has been revealed that aroura brings together an international panel of leading experts in soil science, economics, law, and social science to develop the scientific evidence and policy frameworks needed for a convention. It hosted the Third Global Soil Security Summit at the University of Sydney from October 20 to 23, 2026.

“Soil underpins our food systems, biodiversity, water security and climate resilience, yet it remains largely invisible in international environmental governance,” noted co-author Professor McBratney, a leading international soil scientist who was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2026.

In a recent development, “Through Aroura, we are working to build the scientific and policy foundations for a global convention that recognizes soil as a shared responsibility. We have the knowledge and the tools. What we need now is international commitment.”.

In a recent development, reference: “One Soil, One Planet, No Treaty” by Quentin Styc and Alex McBratney, 3 November 2026, European Journal of Soil Science. DOI: 10.1111/ejss.70448.

Funding was received from the Australian Research Council.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again: Every holiday table needs a salad. This one was dreamed up for Hanukkah, my family’s second-favorite special occasion after Thanksgiving. Serve it with roast chicken or salmon and you have an objectively perfect meal. It’s bright, crunchy, and decked out with little “latkes.” Potato croutons have popped up in a few places over the years, like The Salad Lab’s own Hanukkah-inspired salad (great minds!), Daniel Humm’s salmon rösti salad from Made Nice, and Ore-Ida’s cutely named CrouTots. My take is as lazy as it gets: frozen tater tots, smashed. The result is ultra-crisp, like the tiniest potato pancake in the world. A salad spinner is a godsend for washing the lettuce and herbs. Any type of apple works (I like Honeycrisp or Fuji) and the fresh horseradish on top is optional. But if you can find it, get it!

More festive Hanukkah recipes this way.

Preheat oven to 425°. Mix together ½ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. drained prepared horseradish, 1 Tbsp. distilled white vinegar, a big pinch of kosher salt, and 1 tsp. water in a small bowl, adding more water a little at a time if needed until dressing it drizzle-able. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Bake 1 lb. frozen tater tots on a large rimmed baking sheet for half the time of package directions (about 10 minutes).

It has been revealed that meanwhile, place 1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, in a small bowl; pour in cold water to cover and add a few ice cubes. Set onions aside.

Recent findings suggest that tear pull apart leaves from 1 lb. romaine lettuce (about ⅔ head) and/or Little Gem lettuce (4–5 heads) and tear large leaves in half. Place in a large bowl. Remove tough stems from 1 bunch dill and 1 bunch parsley; discard. Coarsely tear remaining leaves and tender stems. Add to lettuce.

In a recent development, remove tater tots from oven and, using oven mitts for safety, lay another baking sheet directly on top; firmly press down on tots to flatten. (If you don’t have a second baking sheet, use a heatproof measuring cup or mug instead.) Return tater tots to oven and bake until deep golden brown and crisp, 10–20 minutes.(If your oven has a convection setting, now is a great time to use it.).

It has been revealed that drain reserved onion and pat dry. Thinly slice 2 large apples (about 1 lb.). Add both to bowl with lettuce and herbs.

Drizzle 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and add a major pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to combine, then mound salad on a platter. Evenly scatter tater tots and ¾ cup pomegranate seeds over.

Serve salad with remaining dressing for drizzling over and peeled fresh horseradish (if using) for grating over.

💡 Key Takeaways
