Your Personality May Be Partly Written in Your DNA, Massive Study of 1 Million People Reveals

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.
  • Industry observers note that could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others?
  • In a recent development, researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.

Industry observers note that could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others? A large international study suggests that some of the personality traits that make us who we are may be partly rooted in our genes, raising a fascinating question about how much of our personality is determined before we are even born.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people. Published in the journal Nature, the findings offer new insight into how genetics contributes to differences in personality, while also showing why DNA alone cannot explain who we become.

The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99.9% identical. Differences in the remaining 0.1% help influence characteristics such as appearance, disease risk, and responses to medication. The new research suggests that these small genetic differences are also associated with five major dimensions of personality: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.

Industry observers note that scientists have known for decades that both genetics and life experiences influence personality. Finding the specific genetic differences involved has been much more difficult because personality is shaped by many genes, each contributing an extremely small effect. Detecting those subtle patterns requires enormous amounts of data.

Between 2021 and 2022, the Estonian Biobank gathered personality information from nearly 80,000 participants. Although substantial for Estonia, that sample was not large enough to reliably identify many of the genetic associations researchers were looking for.

The University of Tartu team therefore combined its findings with 45 other international datasets, creating a more geographically diverse study population. For certain personality traits, the researchers could analyze data from as many as 1.1 million people. The Estonian sample was the third-largest of all participating groups and used the most comprehensive personality questionnaire.

Industry observers note that the genetic associations were remarkably consistent across different populations, including people of varying ages and geographical backgrounds. However, the identified variants explained only about 4.8% to 9.3% of the differences in personality traits.

Industry observers note that that relatively small proportion highlights how much remains unexplained. Social relationships, environmental influences, and personal experiences may all play substantial roles, along with the ways these factors interact with a person’s genetic makeup.

One particularly interesting feature of the Estonian research allowed scientists to examine personality from two perspectives. Participants could evaluate their own personalities and invite someone who knew them to provide an independent assessment.

“No other biobank in the world offers such an opportunity!” said Uku Vainik, Professor of Behavioral Genetics at the University of Tartu.

According to recent reports, this approach helped researchers address an important question about personality research. Are genetic associations connected to characteristics that other people can actually observe, or do they mainly reflect how individuals think about themselves?

The researchers found substantial overlap between the genetic signals associated with self-reported personality traits and those identified through assessments by acquaintances.

“This reveals that measurable personality traits are truly real, publicly observable characteristics of people, rather than merely individuals’ own opinions about themselves,” explained René Mõttus, Professor of Personality Psychology and co-lead of the study.

The findings are also opening new avenues for understanding the relationship between personality and physical health.

Kerli Ilves, a junior research fellow, is investigating whether personality traits may have causal connections to health-related behaviors, including those associated with body weight, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Her preliminary findings suggest that personality could influence these behaviors, although the relationship may also work in the opposite direction.

Established behavioral patterns might themselves contribute to changes in personality over time.

“We especially see this kind of relationship in smoking,” Ilves noted.

Researchers emphasize that these early findings do not yet establish cause and effect. Understanding whether personality shapes health habits, whether those habits alter personality, or whether both processes occur will require additional research.

“The next step is to use other methods, such as longitudinal studies, to determine whether changes in personality are accompanied by changes in health behavior, and vice versa,” explained Vainik.

The Estonian Biobank is planning another study focused on personality and cognitive functioning. By examining how personality develops and interacts with everyday behavior, researchers hope to better understand what influences people’s health choices and eventually support more effective, personalized approaches to healthy living.

#112400. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1268 w)

The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • In a recent development, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever fresh ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

In a recent development, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever fresh ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

According to recent reports, every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Sources indicate that why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

In a recent development, nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Industry observers note that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

In a recent development, this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Breaking: Scientists Discover That Young Chimpanzees May Develop Accents Just Like Humans

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (446 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.
  • Young chimpanzees may develop something resembling regional accents, with the sounds they make becoming increasingly different depending on the community in which they grow up.
  • In a recent development, much like people who pick up subtle differences in speech from those around them, chimpanzees appear to develop population-specific vocal patterns as they mature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.

Young chimpanzees may develop something resembling regional accents, with the sounds they make becoming increasingly different depending on the community in which they grow up.

In a recent development, much like people who pick up subtle differences in speech from those around them, chimpanzees appear to develop population-specific vocal patterns as they mature. The finding challenges the long-held belief that their calls are largely fixed by genetics from birth.

According to recent reports, A research team led by doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian from the School of Biological and Behavioural Sciences at Queen Mary University of London, in collaboration with the University of Portsmouth, compared the vocalizations of infant and juvenile chimpanzees from two geographically separated populations. By examining grunts, whimpers, and laughter, the researchers found that differences between the groups became more pronounced as the animals grew older.

Not all of these differences appeared at the same time. Some population-specific vocal characteristics were already detectable during infancy, while others emerged as the chimpanzees entered their juvenile years. This provides the first evidence that differences in chimpanzee vocalizations become increasingly distinct throughout early development.

In a recent development, “Understanding how communication develops during early life is fundamental to understanding animal behavior. Our findings show that chimpanzee vocalizations are not simply fixed from birth but continue to develop as young animals interact with their social and ecological environments,” says doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian.

Sources indicate that social interactions, environmental conditions, and other influences beyond genetics may therefore help shape how young chimpanzees communicate. Although the research does not establish precisely how these factors contribute to vocal development, the findings suggest that inherited traits alone cannot explain the differences between populations.

Sources indicate that the discovery does not mean chimpanzees possess language or human-like speech, which involves an agreed vocabulary and grammar. Instead, it offers a new perspective on how communication develops in primates and how vocal patterns can differ between animal communities.

Recent findings suggest that by examining communication at different stages of early life rather than simply comparing adults from different populations, the research provides a framework for investigating how communication systems emerge and diversify. It could also help scientists better understand the biological and environmental influences that shape vocal behavior across other species and the evolution of increasingly complex communication systems.

Reference: “Ontogeny of dialects across chimpanzee vocalisations” by Kassandra Giragosian, Marina Davila-Ross and Derry Taylor, 2 September 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0355313.

Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.
  • But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability.
  • The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

Dried nutmeg. Credit: Wikipedia.

But as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â.

Recent findings suggest that and even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

It has been revealed that by 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

To that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

According to recent reports, A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

According to recent reports, iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he claims.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

Recent findings suggest that over the past 30 years, NASAâs looks for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, indicates Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this fresh ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

#112396. A 360-Year-Old Manuscript Reveals Galileo May Have Built a Telescope Far Ahead of Its Time

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1021 w)

A 360-Year-Old Manuscript Reveals Galileo May Have Built a Telescope Far Ahead of Its Time

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.
  • In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities.
  • According to recent reports, the account was discovered by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.

In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities. A powerful colonial official handed him a telescope and demanded a detailed explanation of how it worked. Nearly 360 years later, the account he produced has resurfaced with a remarkable claim: the instrument was made by Galileo Galilei, and its design may be far more advanced than historians previously believed possible for his time.

According to recent reports, the account was discovered by Dr. José María Moreno Madrid, a researcher at the University of Limerick’s School of History and Geography in Ireland, while examining a manuscript written by Dominican friar Ignacio Muñoz. Dated 1666 and titled De Tellescopiis Stellarum, the document describes a four-lens telescope that Muñoz identified with the Latin phrase “fabricatum a Galilaeo,” meaning “manufactured by Galileo.”.

Industry observers note that the description is unusually precise. Muñoz documented the telescope’s individual components, including its reverse-tapered body and an arrangement of four lenses that allowed distant objects to appear upright. His account describes an erecting eyepiece and convex lenses separated by twice their focal lengths, accompanied by detailed diagrams and drawings that show how the instrument was constructed.

These technical details matter because historical records have generally placed the earliest four-lens telescopes around 1643 to 1645, with their production becoming widespread across Europe beginning in the 1640s. If the instrument really came from Galileo’s workshop, the timeline of telescope development would need to be reconsidered.

In research published in Annals of Science, Moreno Madrid explains what the attribution could mean.

It has been revealed that “If, as the text claims, the telescope analyzed was indeed manufactured by Galileo, then the earliest known experimentation with four-lens telescopes would have to be pushed back to 1630 at the latest and credited to him. Moreover, Muñoz’s De Tellescopiis Stellarum would become the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made by Galileo – and, somewhat paradoxically, it would concern a four-lens telescope rather than the Galilean design that ultimately came to bear his name,” remarked Dr. Moreno Madrid.

The circumstances surrounding Muñoz’s examination provide another intriguing piece of the story. After traveling from Spain to the Philippines, he became involved in an illicit attempt to establish a upcoming Dominican religious order and was subsequently exiled to Portuguese India. Hoping to return to Spain, he contacted King Philip IV with a proposal that promised to improve the performance of Spanish fleets operating around the world.

Muñoz offered his nautical innovation in exchange for royal sponsorship of his journey home aboard the Manila Galleon, which traditionally stopped in Fresh Spain, a Spanish colonial territory. His proposal, however, attracted suspicion from Antonio Sebastián de Toledo Molina y Salazar, the viceroy of New Spain and Marquis of Mancera.

The viceroy questioned whether Muñoz possessed the scientific knowledge he claimed and worried that the friar was simply trying to persuade the king to pay for his travels. To test his abilities, Mancera presented him with the telescope and ordered him to examine it thoroughly. That assignment produced the technical description Moreno Madrid has now brought to light.

Determining whether Galileo actually manufactured the instrument is more complicated. Although the astronomer famously maintained that he had never sold a telescope and never intended to, very few instruments from his lifetime survive with reliable records of their origins. Of the eight surviving telescopes manufactured during the first half of the seventeenth century, none can be attributed to Galileo beyond dispute. Two preserved in the Museum of Florence have traditionally been credited to him, although that identification is not universally accepted. Galileo also left no technical analyses of his own telescopes.

There is, however, a possible connection between Galileo and the Spanish official who possessed Muñoz’s instrument.

Sources indicate that historical accounts indicate that Galileo presented three telescopes, one large and two smaller instruments, to Philip IV and his wife. He hoped to gain favor with the Spanish court and improve his chances of receiving a substantial reward offered for solving the “problem of longitude,” the longstanding difficulty of determining a ship’s east-west position while navigating at sea.

In a recent development, the optical designs of those three telescopes remain unknown, leaving open the possibility that one was the four-lens instrument described by Muñoz. Moreno Madrid suggests that the Spanish royal family may have later given it to Mancera in recognition of his diplomatic and political achievements.

“I believe that the unambiguous attribution of the telescope in the manuscript, together with the documentary evidence that three telescopes made by Galileo – whose optical configuration remain unspecified – may have been accessible to Mancera through his connections at the Spanish court, at the very least invites consideration of this possibility.”.

No further reference to the telescope appears in Mancera’s surviving correspondence with the Spanish court, making Muñoz’s manuscript the only known document connecting this particular instrument to Galileo.

Moreno Madrid also points to Muñoz’s background in mathematics and astronomy as an important reason to take his technical account seriously. The manuscript describes an optical arrangement absent from existing documentation produced by or associated with Galileo and his contemporaries. Regardless of whether the attribution can ultimately be confirmed, it offers historians a rare opportunity to examine seventeenth-century telescope construction in detail. It also illustrates how these instruments served as prestigious possessions among Europe’s political and scientific elites.

For now, the identity of the telescope’s maker remains an open question, one that Moreno Madrid hopes further discoveries will help resolve.

“It is to be hoped that newly introduced documentary or material evidence will soon emerge to confirm the telescope’s attribution and further enhance our understanding of it.”.

Reference: “De Tellescopiis Stellarum (1666). Was Galileo experimenting with four-lens terrestrial telescopes by 1630?” by José María Moreno Madrid, 12 May 2026, Annals of Science. DOI: 10.1080/00033790.2026.2661195.

Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that.
  • Mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once.
  • The strategy starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any plans to release it in a paid journal as part of the âOpen Scienceâ policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details âMars Seedâ - a fresh architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

Mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once. One of the most notable is weight. According to the paper, the entire system weighs in at 20 metric tons - well below the threshold of Martian payloads for Starship or NASAâs proposed 25 ton Mars landers. And crucially, rather than relying on sugar or chemical inputs from Earth, the entire system wonât need any further input from our home planet once it is established on the Red one.

The strategy starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits. Immediately after landing, an autonomous rover sets about unloading the packageâs hardware and assembling a 40kW nuclear fission reactor modeled on the compact nuclear reactors NASA is already developing for Mars and Moon missions. About a month later, the reactor should be fully up and running, providing both electricity and âwasteâ heat that can be used to climate control a habitat.

In a recent development, fraser interviews Dr. Congrui Jin about using bioreactors to grow Martian habitats.

Or in the case of this particular mission structure, to melt some ice. The system would put the heat from the nuclear reactor into a Rodriguez well - a type of ice-drilling technique that melts a pocket of underground ice and pumps the liquid water to the surface, which has already been proven in Antarctica.

Water is a crucial component in the entire systemâs operation. Once the first supply of it has been obtained from the âRodwellâ as itâs known, the system uses a scaled-up version of the urine-recycling system at the moment in place on the International Space Station (ISS) to recover around 90 percent of the water from each production batch of material.

In a recent development, but water isnât the only component input from Mars itself - another is dirt, or âregolithâ in the language of space exploration. The paper estimates the system will require around four tons of Martian soil deposited into its hoppers every day. This could be collected by autonomous mining machines, like NASAâs RASSOR. Approximately 800 kg of that dirt is then stirred into water-filled mixing tanks to dissolve out nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen. But that still leaves the most deadly component of Martian soil - perchlorates.

Fraser interviews Dr. Michael Hecht, one of the main scientists behind the MOXIE experiment to create oxygen out of the atmosphere of Mars.

While these would kill a normal microorganism, Pioneer Labsâ speciality is designing biological systems for use in space exploration. So they simply evolved a hardy strain of the bacterium Cupriavidus necator, which they call sPL.001, which can thrive in the equivalent of a perchlorate-laced broth of Martian regolith simulant back on Earth. That bacterium is also the key engine in creating the bioplastics that are used to 3D print the radiation-shielded habitats.

Sources indicate that bacteria need food though, and shipping it from Earth would be prohibitively expensive. So thereâs one final input to the system from the Red Planet - its atmosphere. The first step in that process is an upgraded version of the MOXIE experiment that successfully showed an ability to split the carbon dioxide in Marsâ atmosphere into carbon monoxide and oxygen.

Typically, that system simply gets rid of the carbon monoxide to capture the oxygen for use in rocket fuel. But in Mars Seed, carbon monoxide is actually the prize. Using a technique inspired by an emerging field called âelectro-agriculture,â the system combines waste carbon monoxide gas with water to produce liquid acetic acid - the main ingredient in vinegar.

Fraser talks in detail about what we can find to live off of when we eventually do send humans to the Red Planet.

According to recent reports, while a diet of straight vinegar might not sound appealing to a human, to a microbe it's nourishing enough. In four separate 1,000L fermentation tanks, the engineered microbes eat this vinegar, combined with oxygen, packing themselves with a bioplastic called polyhydroxybutyrate, with the polymer eventually making up 70% of their body weight. At that point, a high-speed centrifuge harvests the bacteria cells from the liquid broth, and the resulting paste is split into two separate assembly lines.

Half of the raw paste is mixed with Martian dirt and fed into a giant gantry 3D printer, which then extrudes a corrugated, arched outer protective shell. Rovers then work to pile around 2m of dirt onto the outer shell, creating a barrier to the cosmic rays and micrometeorites that plague the Martian surface.

Recent findings suggest that the other half of the bacteria is subjected to a pressure bath of liquid carbon dioxide, again pulled straight from the atmosphere. This extracts the pure bioplastic, which is then melted and spun into an airtight, reinforced inner tent that is capable of holding a breathable atmosphere.

In a recent development, interview with Dr. Erika DeBenedictis, the founder of Pioneer Labs. Credit - The New Biology YouTube Channel.

According to recent reports, so, in essence, this 20 ton system can be dropped on Mars, including a pair of helping rovers, and extract all of the necessary components to continually and consistently build atmosphere-tight, safe shelter for astronauts, at a rate of about 75 sq meters every 130 days. The paper notes that, comparing the system to directly launching 20 tons of pre-made plastic building materials from Earth, the break-even point of the stand-alone biofabrication facility is around 1,400 Martian days - which lines up nicely with the two orbital alignment cycles NASA is planning to utilize before sending human crews.

In a recent development, the main difference is that the biofabrication facility never stops producing those safe habitats, which clearly is a major advantage. Despite its promise, though, there are still plenty of engineering challenges to overcome before this system will be anywhere near launch ready. But, when that time comes, it appears that we might be able to literally grow safe habitats out of Martian water, air, and soil. And that is something any future mission planner will be thrilled to have as an option.

D. A. Stork et al - Mars Seed: A Reference Architecture for Biomanufacturing Habitats from Martian Resources.

Fresh Congress will still be filled with losers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct.
  • OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.
  • Sources indicate that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

Sources indicate that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

Industry observers note that I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown declared his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

In a recent development, brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

It has been revealed that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Newly introduced Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

According to recent reports, but they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

Sources indicate that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

It has been revealed that we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Latest to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he debuted Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Sources indicate that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he released Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

According to recent reports, eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

Industry observers note that this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

It has been revealed that ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

Recent findings suggest that these days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Recent findings suggest that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

Recent findings suggest that the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The newly introduced online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

It has been revealed that at the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Fresh York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

Industry observers note that while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most notable British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand newly introduced, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

In a recent development, must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

It has been revealed that shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

According to recent reports, for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Industry observers note that gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Recent findings suggest that mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a significant group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

In a recent development, A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips claims Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in newly introduced-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Sources indicate that possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Industry observers note that fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Latest Update: Researchers Just Sent an Unblockable Message Through a Solid Wall Using Gravity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.
  • Industry observers note that physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals.
  • The experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.

Industry observers note that physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals. Their unconventional communication system relied on a moving elevator counterweight and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in the gravitational field.

The experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter positioned in a nearby bathroom detected the gravitational changes and decoded a single word: “Gravity.”.

Unlike radio waves and other electromagnetic signals, gravitational fields cannot be blocked by ordinary building materials. This means information carried by changes in gravity could potentially reach places where conventional wireless communication struggles.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ’s School of Mathematics and Physics explained the advantage. “Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” he noted. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”.

The communication experiment grew out of an unrelated effort to measure vehicle weights without physical contact. Dr. Andrew Groszek and his colleagues were developing a system that could estimate the mass of trucks and other heavy vehicles by detecting their gravitational attraction.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr. Groszek remarked. “Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”.

The researchers applied that principle to communication by moving a large mass between fixed positions. Each movement altered the gravitational field measured by the detector, allowing the team to encode binary information without transmitting electromagnetic signals.

It has been revealed that although the experiment successfully transmitted information, its data rate was exceptionally low. Professor Andrew White identified the aging elevator as a major constraint.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White remarked.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.”.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”.

Professor Matthew Davis noted the experiment established that information can be deliberately encoded in a gravitational field and recovered by a detector. The achievement demonstrates the underlying physics, although substantial improvements would be needed before the technique could serve as a useful communication system.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely upcoming way of communicating,” Professor Davis remarked. “We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.”.

The researchers also modeled how more sensitive quantum sensors might improve the technique. Unlike the classical gravimeter used in the experiment, such sensors could potentially detect weaker gravitational changes at greater distances.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (about 1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”.

In a recent development, those figures are theoretical projections, not experimentally demonstrated capabilities. Gravity-based communication remains far too slow for practical applications, but more advanced detectors could eventually make it possible to exchange information in environments that radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

It has been revealed that reference: “Unblockable communication with gravity” by Andrew J. Groszek, Charles W. Woffinden, Michael D. Harvey, Andrew G. White and Matthew J. Davis, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee0802.

#112391. LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets
