📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first of its kind instrument shows its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.

The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative fresh instrument.

A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Located on the Mercury Planetary Orbiter segment of the BepiColombo spacecraft stack, UK-built MIXS is the first x-ray instrument on an interplanetary spacecraft, and UK Space Agencyâs instrument contribution to the mission.

In a recent development, the image reveals the Crab Nebula (Messier 1) in x-ray light. Located 6,500 light-years distant, âThe Crabâ is a prominent x-ray source, located 6,500 light-years distant in the constellation of Taurus the Bull. The Crab Nebula made a fine target for calibration and testing. Itâs rare for an interplanetary mission to deliberately image a deep-sky object, though they do occasionally turn up in star-tracker navigation frames.

According to recent reports, MIXS image of the Crab Nebula (inset) overlaid on a visible light background. Credit:ESA/University of Leicester/NASA/GSFC.

New Horizons once captured the âWishing Wellâ open cluster NGC 3532 using its LORRI imager.

Industry observers note that âX-rays cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere to the ground so all X-ray telescopes must be in space,â Adam Fox (MIXS Operations Scientist) told Universe Today. âX-rays can only be reflected to a focus at very shallow angles, which means conventional X-ray telescopes must have very long focal lengths (~10 meters) with nested mirrors, meaning a mass of hundreds of kilograms.â.

âMIXS uses novel X-ray optics called micro-pore optics which have millions of tiny pores (20 microns wide) to allow an X-ray telescope which is 1 meter in length and weighs only 11 kilograms, making it small and light enough to be flown to Mercury.â.

Industry observers note that the MIXS instrument had to wait through 8-long years of space travel, until the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) was jettisoned from the stack joined to the Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) and the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) this past September 3rd. This finally exposed MIXS to space, allowing the team an opportunity to calibrate and test the instrument prior to arrival.

Sources indicate that the BepiColombo spacecraft stack prior to launch. Credit: ESA.

âUntil early September, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) which carries MIXS was attached to the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) which provided power and propulsion during BepiColombo's 8 year cruise to Mercury,â says Fox. âDuring this time, MIXS' view was directly blocked by the transfer module, only following this separation has MIXS had a view of deep space for the first time. MIXS has been switched on periodically during cruise for checkouts of instrument health during which only the behavior of the detectors within could be monitored.â.

The image is the result of 55 platform slews over the course of 39 hours on September 11 and 12th shortly after MTM disposal.

In a recent development, MIXS is designed to create a surface map showing the atomic makeup of Mercury at an unprecedented scale. Working in tandem with the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), MIXS will look at fluorescence of surface material created as a result of high energy solar x-rays impacting the surface. MIXS will also document the local environment in x-rays and magnetospheric interaction on the nighttime side of the planet.

The MIXS instrument prior to launch. Credit: University of Leicester.

âThe scientific advantage from having an X-ray telescope at Mercury is that (the) surface emits X-rays when hit by Solar X-rays or particles from the magnetosphere,â Alec McCrea (University of Leicester) told Universe Today. âThese X-rays have characteristic energies corresponding to certain elements which can tell you what the surface is made of. An X-ray telescope can achieve this at a much higher resolution than achieved on previous missions due to both its smaller FOV and imaging capabilities.â.

The arrival for the BepiColombo mission at Mercury occurred late last week on November 21st, when Mercury finally captured the attached MMO and MPO pair into an initial elliptical orbit, after a close 635 kilometer pass above the surface of the planet.

This marked a first a âweak stability captureâ for a planetary mission, as BepiColombo moved inside the gravitational influence of Mercury. The thruster fire was also a first for the spacecraft stack post transfer module separation in September.

There was a bit of drama last week as Estrack controllers noted the mission briefly entered safe mode and the planned thruster burn ended prematurely. The spacecraft still achieved 77% of the expected velocity change, enough to enter orbit. BepiColombo is now in a 75 hour orbit around Mercury, versus the original planned 58 hour orbit.

This comes after one Earth, two Venus and six flybys past Mercury needed to enter capture and orbit around the innermost world. The arrival was also extended from December 2025 to this month, due to an issue with the thrusters on the MTM. This is JAXAâs and ESAâs first mission to Mercury, and only the second to orbit the innermost world since NASAâs Messenger mission ended operations on April 30, 2015, becoming the first human-made object to impact Mercury.

The first mission to see Mercury closeup was NASAâs Mariner 10 on 1974.

The timeline for BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury. Credit: ESA.

It has been revealed that next comes the release of JAXAâs MMO (Mio) orbiter on December 9-10th, followed by the sun-shield ejection on December 16th. MPO will then settle down into a 480 by 1500 kilometer orbit early next year on March 10th, after which science operations can finally begin on April 6th. BepiColombo is expected to operate around Mercury until the end of the nominal mission in April 2028, with a possible extension until December 2029.

âDevelopment of such instruments is active. For planetary X-ray fluorescence, a MIXS-like instrument is applicable to many airless bodies in the solar system and would be tailored as such,â says Fox. âMicropore optic X-ray telescopes though have since been flown on several astrophysics missions, including SMILE, Einstein Probe and the (Space Variable Objects Monitor) SVOM.â.

Sources indicate that if youâre up early this week, you can spot Mercury and wave at BepiColombo as well. The planet just passed greatest elongation west of the Sun this past weekend, and sits just below brilliant Venus at dawn.

Itâll be exciting to see what results BepiColombo and MIXS produce as they get down to work in 2027.

Researchers Have Discovered a Previously Unknown Crystal Form of Silver

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.
  • It has been revealed that silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form.
  • The findings, published in Nano Letters, emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.

It has been revealed that silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form. Researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a previously unknown crystal arrangement in which silver atoms form a simple cubic pattern, a structure previously documented in only one other element.

The findings, published in Nano Letters, emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale. Unlike ordinary silver, the newly formed crystals began converting into silver oxide within approximately 100 seconds, demonstrating how dramatically atomic arrangement can influence a material’s chemical behavior.

Most silver crystallizes in a structure known as face-centered cubic, in which atoms occupy the eight corners and the center of each face of a repeating cube. This tightly packed arrangement is also found in common metals such as gold, copper, and aluminum.

In a recent development, the newly discovered silver instead formed a simple cubic structure, with atoms occupying only the corners of each repeating cube. This arrangement is exceptionally uncommon in pure elements. Before this discovery, the only known elemental example was radioactive polonium, whose simple cubic structure was identified in 1966.

“It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal,” says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. “We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn’t expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure.”.

The researchers created and examined the silver using a transmission electron microscope (TEM), which employs electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light to resolve structures down to individual atoms. The electron beam served two purposes: it triggered the decomposition of silver iodide and allowed the scientists to watch the resulting silver atoms organize into crystals.

Sources indicate that the nanoscale conditions were essential to the discovery. At dimensions of just a few billionths of a meter, materials can temporarily adopt crystal structures that would be unstable in larger samples. Such arrangements can produce physical and chemical properties that differ substantially from those of the same element in its conventional form.

Industry observers note that experiments conducted under high vacuum revealed a striking difference between the two silver structures. Conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, while the simple cubic crystals gradually oxidized, forming silver oxide. The rapid transformation provided direct evidence of the new structure’s unusually high chemical reactivity.

“Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide,” adds Sakakibara.

The researchers believe their technique could provide a way to discover other previously unknown crystal structures and investigate the properties they produce.

“This is a fresh approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future,” claims Professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University.

“Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Electron-Beam-Assisted Formation of Simple-Cubic Silver” by Masaya Sakakibara, Hiroki Nada, Yuji Kunisada, Tomoya Yamazaki and Yuki Kimura, 4 November 2026, Nano Letters. DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03635.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that there are two types of people who have a paper shredder at home: Most folks are what I like to think of as “casual” shredders, who shred paper bank statements, medical notices, snail mail credit-card or life insurance offers from time to time. Home-office workers, gig workers and freelancers, small business owners, retirees, and anyone wary of identity theft. Then there are the “serious” shredders—doctors, lawyers, accountants, government workers, or anyone who regularly handles no-one-else-needs-to-know information—who may need to obliterate foot-high stacks of documents day after day, which requires a powerful, secure, durable machine that can monotonously masticate without jamming or overheating.

Whether you’re a “casual” or “serious” shredder, everyone wants to find a home office workshop that doesn’t cost too much but can handle their workload swiftly, smoothly, and securely. Within both camps, there are significant features that can make or break a shredder: longer run and shorter cooldown times, bigger bins, quieter motors, safety features, casters, and compact designs that let you tuck an infrequently used shredder discreetly under your desk. There are also special features that can make life easier, like anti-jam protections and solutions, ever-smaller particles, and automatic paper feeding. It’s easy to pick a paper shredder, bring it home, and hope for the best: But if you’re reading this guide, chances are you’d rather not leave your information security to chance.

And that’s why we’ve tested many of the most popular shredders on the market. We’ve found the best options for a wide spectrum of specialties. Whether you need to crush a foot-high pile of papers every morning or a few envelopes every week, we’ve found a shredder whose power, capacity, conveniences, and price all cater to your needs.

In a recent development, paper shredders are more home office tech than conventional consumer electronics: Most of us don’t plan on upgrading our paper shredders regularly. As a result, the tech inside evolves far more slowly than gear like laptops, phones, and even printers. As a result, many of the best models stay at the top of the heap for years.

Given that reality, I try to look for the best of the best, not the “latest and greatest.” Ideally these are machines that you can invest in and trust to meet your needs for years and years. In fact, I’ve owned and used my personal shredder, an old Fellowes MS-450Cs shredder, for two decades.

While selecting which shredders match specific purposes for this guide, we considered mostly real-world factors as well as tech specs, such as:.

Industry observers note that since our last roundup, I’ve tested an expanding range of models, from cheap shredder-mechanism-over-trash-bin designs to full-fledged micro-cut and auto-feed machines. I also widened my search beyond familiar shredder brands to lesser-known and retailer-exclusive models where performance, features, price, and consumer history warranted consideration. Some of these often-unknown brands can be surprisingly difficult to contact, which makes where a shredder is sold—and what help that retailer provides if something goes wrong—part of our value equation.

The Fellowes Powershred LX220 is the most versatile shredder I’ve tested, and works equally well in a home office, pulverizing an occasional pile of household paperwork, or tackling the more substantial workload of a professional team. My testing revealed its stated specs met or even exceeded its rated 20-sheet capacity and 30-minute runtime. Plus, Fellowes’ IntelliBar provides visual feedback on bin fullness, runtime, and sheet capacity, while SafeSense stops the cutters when hands approach the paper opening.

Best of all, Fellowes’ proactive “100-percent Jam Proof” system is designed to detect overambitious stacks and head off paper jam interruptions before they happen.

Notice, I noted designed to. During our testing, we did manage to jam the supposedly 100-percent-jam-proof LX220. In its defense, I was actively trying to choke it rather than accidentally overstuffing it in a fit of shredding enthusiasm.

Under more normal conditions, Fellowes’ anti-jam system works incredibly well. Combined with the LX220’s other talents and relatively few shortcomings, it’s still the shredder we’d recommend to the widest variety of buyers.

For $75, the Sam’s Club-exclusive Member’s Mark C249-A delivers a robust set of functional and convenience-minded features, including some options you’d expect only on a higher-priced shredder.

It has a rather surprising skill set, anchored by a 12-sheet capacity, P-4 micro-cut security, 30-minute runtime, and an auto-reverse to help clear jams. It also has a “safety interlock/shred safe” feature—a helpful safety precaution that prevents operation when the bin is missing or not seated correctly. It’s common in high-end shredders, but a huge get at this price.

Surprisingly, it also handles nearly all the non-paper office detritus likely to find its way into a shredder—staples, credit cards, CDs, and what Sam’s Club describes as “small” paper clips. Again, this kind of power is normally reserved for more expensive models.

Not only do you get capacity, stamina, security, and convenience for not a lot of money, but you have the convenience of taking it back to Sam’s Club if something should go wrong with it.

If your shredding needs lean toward the occasional, choose one that won’t hog otherwise valuable floor space. Better yet, get a shredder that’s essentially invisible when not in use. At roughly 15 inches tall, and barely a foot wide, this compact Aurora AU870MZ may not be a ninja, but its ability to simply slide beneath your desktop makes it as unobtrusive as a shredder can be.

Not only does this Aurora—not to be confused with its older and less capable sibling, the AU870MA—disappear beneath most desks or easily slip into a closet, it can also make up to eight sheets disappear at a time.

There are some compromises. This Aurora’s 3.9-gallon bin will fill faster, and its five-minute runtime won’t be enough time to take care of even a small pile of accumulated scraps in one session. But if you consider this a JIC shredder, being able to hide it is likely more crucial to you than its lack of workhorse attributes.

Recent findings suggest that while compact, this Aurora doesn’t skimp on shredding security or capability. You get a P-4 micro-cutting mechanism that also can chomp non-paper credit cards, staples, and small paper clips.

Industry observers note that nearly everyone would rather do almost any other kind of office work than shredding. So, instead of feeding and watching, this HP (made by Royal and sometimes listed as the 91032T and/or the AF809) lets you load up to 80 sheets into its clever fold up/down automatic feeder which frees you up to do something more important, like grab a snack or cup of coffee.

However, in the real world, the small 3.8-gallon bin doesn’t hold the bits from all 80 shredded pages without some help. Once I reached around 50 pages shredded, the HP stopped and waited until I pulled out the bin and leveled its shredded contents. After shoving the bin back in, the HP finished the remaining 30 pages without any trouble. But even with this bin shuffling, the 80 sheets got chewed up in just around five minutes.

Other than its mismatched auto-feed and bin capacities, this surprisingly affordable, speedy, and compact machine—it’s less than 17 inches tall—includes P-4 micro-cut security and can also masticate credit cards, staples, paper clips, and CDs through its 9-sheet manual feed slot.

If you’re the paranoid type—rather extra extra careful like me—about completely obliterating confidential documents—purchase a shredder that’s capable of mincing personal papers into the most minuscule, irrecoverable particles possible at a price that doesn’t require a bond issue.

The relatively fresh Effeluviate Q9 deploys P-7 cutters—a shredding security level normally associated with much pricier specialist machines and here for something approaching a consumer price—pulverizes a document into tiny 1 × 1.7mm particles (3/64 x 5/64, or 0.05 x 0.08, of an inch), a fraction of the size of a P-5 shredder produced particle.

In a recent development, other than its ultra-secure P-7 rating and its resulting paper powder, this Q9’s remaining specs are almost boringly conventional: a relatively low seven-sheet manual feed, a decent 30-minute runtime, and a mid-range 5.23-gallon bin (not 6 gallons, as rated). And while the Q9 can crush plastic credit cards, staples, and CDs, it’s apparently allergic to paper clips.

Its sub-56dB noise rating, however, makes the Q9 about 10dB quieter than most shredders so mincing documents won’t disturb your co-habitants either day or night. I’m a little skittish about recommending a relatively unknown brand, but the specs are incredibly impressive.

It has been revealed that if you must macerate massive masses of documents on a daily basis, the Bonsen S9221 is about to become your fresh best friend. Lift up its top, load up to 320 sheets into its flatbed feeder, and walk away. In 30 minutes, all 320 sheets will be transformed into tiny 2 × 10mm specks.

Industry observers note that the S9221’s 8.1-gallon pull-out bin is appropriately roomy for the kind of 320-sheet jobs its auto feeder invites. Although you can leave large jobs to the auto feeder, a separate manual slot handles up to 10 sheets in smaller batches along with staples, paper clips, and credit cards—but not CDs.

One thing to keep an eye out for when you go to buy: There’s an older version of the S9221 with a slightly lower 300-page capacity and only P-4 micro-cut security instead of P-5. Since it has the same name and similar features to the latest model, it would be very easy to buy the old model without noticing. Please make sure to check the listing before clicking “buy.”.

I recently evaluated the top shredders under $100, and there are a few sub-$100 models that work great and are more widely available than the Member’s Mark, including the Amazon Basics 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($59), the Staples ST62150 ($82), which is loaded with safety features, and the Bonsaii C275-A 12-Sheet Cross-Cut ($65), ideal for infrequent emptying.

Industry observers note that you may not be able to control where your digital data ends up. But you know exactly how you can securely dispose of your paper records. The trick is deciding which shredder will best satisfy your serious or casual shredding needs, which usually comes down to a handful of features.

In a recent development, once you start your shredding chore, you’d rather not be interrupted by problems with your shredder. Runtime tells you how long you can keep feeding paper into a shredder before its motor overheats and shuts down, forcing you to wait 30 to 45 minutes, depending on the model, for the machine to catch its mechanical breath.

A small personal shredder may run for only five or 10 minutes, which is plenty if you dispatch only a few documents at a time. If you’re regularly confronted by larger piles to pulverize, look for a runtime of 30 minutes or more.

Once you choose a shredder with longer runtimes, don’t obsess over the advertised cooldown time. You may fill the bin before the shredder overheats and, by the time you’ve disposed of all that confetti, the motor already has had a chance to cool before you return with an empty bin.

A shredder is still largely a mechanical device, a motor driving a set of cutters, augmented in many models by sensors and electronic controls. And as with any mechanical object, failure is often less a question of if than when. Long-term owner shredder reviews are especially useful for spotting recurring problems with motors, sensors, switches, and other parts that may not misbehave during short-term testing.

Unfortunately, getting help directly from some shredder brands can be harder than clearing a paper jam. During our ongoing shredder research, we’ve encountered multiple manufacturers failing to respond to repeated emails and phone calls. Some brands don’t even provide a U.S. customer-service number.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t automatically make shredders from these contact-resistant brands a bad buy. Purchasing from an established store or online retailer with a clearly stated return or replacement policy gives you a more reliable resource to turn to if your new shredder turns out to be a lemon. Before buying—particularly from an unfamiliar brand—check both the manufacturer’s warranty and especially the retailer’s return/replace policy.

Industry observers note that unlike the shredders you may remember from old movies, most modern machines no longer turn documents into long linguini-like strips. Cross-cut shredders slice paper both lengthwise and crosswise into small rectangular scraps. Micro-cut models slice and dice those scraps into even tinier bits, leaving hundreds or even thousands of petite particles.

Sources indicate that for most home and home-office use, either cutting method provides plenty of protection. Most shredders these days offer micro-cut machines with either P-4 security, which makes reconstructing a document the most puzzling jigsaw puzzle ever, or P-5 security, whose even more diminutive document destruction methods are favored by MDs, CPAs, JDs, or by other professionals with initials in their titles.

The larger and more powerful your shredder, the more sheets it can generally chew through at one time. Just don’t treat the number printed on the box as a dare.

Recent findings suggest that manufacturers’ rated sheet capacities are best-case numbers, usually based on neatly aligned standard-weight bond paper. Thicker stock, folds, staples, uneven piles, and stuffed envelopes can rapidly turn a “12-sheet” machine into something more comfortable with eight or nine. Feeding a few sheets below the rated maximum is one of the easiest ways to avoid jams and unnecessary strain.

Manual shredders require you to stand there feeding paper in batches. Auto-feed machines let you load a stack, walk away, and get something else done while the shredder eats.

In a recent development, here again, don’t take the rated auto-feed sheet capacity too literally. An “80-sheet” or “200-sheet” auto feeder may accommodate that many pristine sheets under ideal conditions, but real paperwork is rarely pristine. Wrinkles, folds, different paper weights, staples, and uneven stacks can reduce how much you can reliably leave it to swallow unattended. Plus, the bin on a high-capacity auto-feed model may fill before the maximum number of sheets are fed into it.

According to recent reports, auto-feed mechanisms also add more rollers, sensors, and jam-clearing compartments. And more moving mechanical parts create more places for something to eventually go wrong.

However, if you routinely accumulate large piles, the time a highly rated auto-feed shredder saves can easily outweigh the added complexity and potential mechanical problems.

A bigger bin means fewer trips to empty it, but gallon capacity tells only part of the story. Pull-out drawers are lighter and easier to clean and empty. Bins that require lifting the often heavy shredder mechanism off the top of a wastepaper basket can potentially scatter loose particles still in the cutter mechanism.

In a recent development, also pay attention to what happens when you pull that drawer out. Paper confetti has an impressive ability to cling to plastic, pile up behind a bin, and otherwise escape the container designed to hold it. An easy-to-remove bin that keeps most of its shredded paper actually in the bin will save you emptying and cleanup aggravation, especially if you don’t wait until the bin is filled to its brim.

Shredders may look sturdy and impervious, but most are actually quite finicky eaters. Nearly every shredder will eventually jam if you feed it too much at one time or feed it the wrong type, shape, or mix of paper. More advanced models with more advanced anti-jam systems sense an overload before one occurs, or either automatically reverse or allow you to manually reverse to relieve the jam before you need to perform paper-removal surgery from the cutters with tweezers or needle-nose pliers.

Recent findings suggest that the cheapest jam protection, however, is restraint. If a machine claims 12 sheets, regularly feeding it eight or nine instead will lower your odds of spending quality time violently tugging mangled paper back out of its teeth.

In a recent development, most current shredders can swallow staples and paper clips, and many can also chew up plastic credit cards. CDs and other thicker media such as metal cards are less universally welcome.

Check the manufacturer’s instructions before you buy for what non-paper materials a shredder can successfully chew and before feeding anything other than paper into its cutters. A shredder capable of mincing a stack of tax records can object like a microwave forced to cook metal—something it wasn’t designed to eat.

Probably less than you think. For most people who dispatch a few bills, receipts, financial statements, or junk-mail offers every few days, well under $100 can buy a perfectly capable shredder.

Spending more generally buys stamina, convenience, and durability: longer runtimes, larger bins, higher sheet capacities, auto-feed, better jam protection, sometimes finer-cut security, and years if not decades of service. Those features become worth paying for as the amount and frequency of your shredding increase.

According to recent reports, as with nearly all things, don’t be penny wise and pound foolish. You will find you will shred more than you anticipated—it’s just human nature to use a latest device more than you though you would. Overall, shredders costing several hundreds of dollars make the most sense for people who regularly devour large stacks or have a specialized need. Don’t decide what to spend simply by asking how private your paperwork is; ask how much of it you need to turn into confetti and how often both now and in the future.

The most notable shredder “spec” may be how little time it forces you to spend with it. Sheet capacity, runtime, security level, and bin capacity are the headline numbers I’d look at first. Runtime is particularly useful because it tells you something about how much work the machine can comfortably handle before demanding a rest.

In a recent development, but some of the things that most determine whether you’ll love or hate a shredder aren’t specs at all. Nearly every decent modern shredder can reduce ordinary documents beyond casual recognition. The bigger differences are how often it jams, how easily those jams clear, how cleanly the bin empties, and how much confetti winds up everywhere except inside it.

In a recent development, check owner reviews for recurring complaints about jams, overheating, finicky sensors, messy bins, and other annoyances. AI agents on online sites can summarize customer reviews to answer many of these before-you-buy questions.

Sources indicate that with shredders, old doesn’t necessarily mean obsolete. Sometimes it means proven.Unlike most consumer electronics, shredders don’t become outdated because they lack this year’s faster processor, fresh operating system, wireless standard, or other bleeding-edge technology. An older model that’s still attracting buyers and good reviews may actually offer something a brand-new machine can’t: years of accumulated evidence about how well it holds up.

Industry observers note that before buying an older model, check whether the manufacturer has introduced a newer or revised version. When shopping online, search the manufacturer’s current lineup or, if the retailer provides an AI or shopping assistant, ask whether there’s a newer version of the model you’re considering. Then compare old to newly introduced rather than automatically assuming new means better.

The best shredder maintenance is self-restraint. Don’t continually stuff the cutters to their rated maximum, allow the bin overflow, or feed the machine materials it wasn’t designed to digest.

Lubrication requirements vary. Some manufacturers recommend shredder oil applied at regular intervals, others suggest pre-lubricated oil sheets, and some models claim to require little or no lubrication at all. Follow the instructions for your particular machine rather than assuming every shredder requires the same type of mechanical TLC.

Beyond that, maintenance should be pretty painless: empty the bin before the paper snow reaches the cutters, occasionally clean dusty sensors if the manufacturer recommends it, and clear jams rather than repeatedly hammering the reverse button and hoping for divine intervention.

Despite the name, most modern “shredders” no longer shred paper into long strips. While cross cut and micro cut are clues for how small the ultimate shred pieces will be, P-ratings, part of the DIN 66399 security standard, put an actual number on “small.”.

It has been revealed that P-ratings run from P-1 through P-7; the higher the number, the smaller the pieces produced. For ordinary household paperwork, P-3 is already plenty secure. A cross-cut P-3 machine reduces a document to hundreds of pieces, which is more than enough discouragement for anyone contemplating reconstructing your bills, junk mail, receipts, or other everyday paperwork. After all, a document pieced back together like a taped mosaic isn’t likely to fool many people.

Sources indicate that P-4 is the sweet spot for buyers who want their paperwork diced considerably finer without spending much more, and P-4 is common among consumer micro-cut shredders. P-5 turns documents into even tinier bits and makes sense for especially sensitive financial, legal, medical, or professional paperwork. P-6 and P-7 go further still, into security levels intended for documents whose contents matter considerably more than last month’s Visa bill.

For most of us, then, P-3 is plenty, P-4 buys extra peace of mind, and P-5 is for paperwork you’d really rather nobody put back together.

In a recent development, stewart Wolpin, based in Fresh York City, has been writing about, reporting on, and reviewing consumer technology for nearly 40 years. He also serves as the unofficial historian for CTA (Consumer Technology Association), the trade group that produces the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), which he has attended and covered since 1984. He is also a huge Beatles fan and a METS season ticket holder.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space.
  • To understand why, letâs look at how engineers currently grade collision risk.
  • Sources indicate that if a manufacturer funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is âsafeâ in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

To understand why, letâs look at how engineers currently grade collision risk. Standards set by NASA and the European Space Agency rely on color-coded charts that sort missions into one of several buckets based on their risk profile. Categories like âLow,â âMedium,â and âHighâ are self-explanatory, but they eliminate vital distinctions in risk profiles, and only look at one satellite at a time. And, crucially, they focus solely on the risk to the tech giant that released them.

Sources indicate that if a manufacturer funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company. But if a mega-constellation operator builds thousands of identical satellites at a cost of a million dollars a pop, losing one barely registers on their financial statements. Consequently, according to the risk profile, all relatively inexpensive, reproducible satellites that make up the mega-constellations end up with a âLowâ risk profile.

Fraser talks about how we make sure satellites don't crash into each other.

The algorithm described in the paper exposes the flaw in that logic by separating the risk into two different scores. First is the âIndividual Riskâ â i.e. the traditional metric of the financial hit a satelliteâs owner takes if the spacecraft is destroyed by collision. The second is the âCollective Riskâ, which ignores the cost of each individual satellite, but captures the physical danger each imposes on every other operational satellite in its altitude band across its entire operational and disposal lifetime.

Sources indicate that mathematically, this is a way of capturing the âtragedy of the commonsâ aspect of orbital space. Economists have long warned that when a âpublic goodâ (such as an orbital path) is free to use, users, whether they are farmers on a field or launch companies trying to build internet satellite constellations, have an incentive to utilize as much of the free resource as they can while not paying any attention to the consequences of that use.

In orbit, those consequences take the form of congestion, dodging maneuvers, and potential destruction of other satellites that are forced on every other organization if one decides to ignore their responsibility to properly manage the impact their equipment has on an orbit. As weâve reported before, those consequences are growing, with an average Starlink satellite having to fire its thruster at least once a week to dodge a potential collision.

Fraser talks about how space junk could eventually block our access to orbit.

Starlink itself is a good case in point. A single Starlink V2 Mini, orbiting at 525 km, has a collective risk 317 times higher than the âindividual risk.â In a traditional risk assessment, this would mark it as âLowâ risk, whereas this fresh framework would place it very clearly in the âVery Highâ camp.

There have been some efforts to capture this long-term environmental impact already. ESA uses an index called the Environmental Consequences of Orbital Breakups (ECOB) and researchers at EPFL in Switzerland have put forward the Space Sustainability Rating. However, the simulations underpinning these metrics are computationally expensive and require hours to complete. The tool Toson developed in MATLAB runs in seconds on a standard computer and matches the higher-end benchmarks exceptionally well.

According to recent reports, itâs all good to simply update the categorization of a satellite for its collective risk, but having that information is useless if operators and regulators donât do anything with it. Toson suggests updating the international debris guidelines and licensing rules to take this new metric into account. If a company wants to launch a low-cost satellite that will affect the orbital environment for everyone else, they should be required to either fund active debris cleanup or accept a cap on the total risk posed by their fleet of spacecraft.

Fraser talks about real-life advanced tech that can remove space debris.

It has been revealed that regulators havenât had much time to digest this newly introduced idea, so donât expect to see any such rules anytime soon. But as our orbital highways become more and more congested, satellite operators will need more guidance on how to maintain the commons before we end up in a Kessler Syndrome situation. This new paper may contribute to that standards-setting â and the sooner the better.

Scientists Discover the Human Ear May Work Very Differently Than We Thought

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists have discovered that low-frequency sounds can produce nearly simultaneous vibrations across widely separated regions of the inner ear.
  • According to recent reports, for decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have discovered that low-frequency sounds can produce nearly simultaneous vibrations across widely separated regions of the inner ear. The finding, observed in guinea pigs, challenges a long-standing model of how hearing works and could influence the development of more advanced cochlear implants.

According to recent reports, for decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map. Different sounds activate different locations along its membrane, much like individual piano keys correspond to specific notes. High frequencies stimulate one end, while low frequencies primarily activate the other. This arrangement, known as the “place code,” has helped explain how the ear distinguishes sounds and forms a foundation of modern cochlear implant technology.

It has been revealed that the traditional model dates back to research by Georg von Békésy, who received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for demonstrating how different sound frequencies stimulate distinct regions of the cochlea. However, the fresh study, published in Science Advances, suggests that this location-based explanation does not fully account for how the inner ear processes low-frequency sounds.

To investigate, researchers used optical coherence tomography (OCT), an imaging technology (co-invented by OHSU physician-scientist David Huang) widely used in eye examinations. Combined with advanced signal processing to reduce background noise, the technique allowed scientists to detect extremely small vibrations at multiple locations inside the guinea pig cochlea.

Sources indicate that the measurements showed that low-frequency sounds produced similar vibrations across distant regions, often with synchronized motion. Rather than disproving the cochlea’s frequency map, the findings indicate that additional mechanisms may contribute to how low-frequency information is represented and interpreted. The results build on earlier research published in 2022 that identified unexpected patterns of low-frequency responses.

Understanding low-frequency hearing is particularly crucial for interpreting complex sounds, including speech. These vibrations are difficult to measure experimentally, and people with hearing loss often struggle to understand conversations when background noise is present.

Industry observers note that “When you bring in low-frequency background noise, it’s a very challenging environment for people with hearing loss,” said George Burwood, Ph.D., the study’s lead author and a research instructor at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). “Also, the place code paradigm limits the interpretation of how mammals evolved to detect extremely complex signals, especially speech.”.

Sources indicate that current cochlear implants use electrodes to electrically stimulate different regions of the cochlea according to sound frequency. The new findings suggest that reproducing more of the natural cochlea’s complex vibration patterns might improve how these devices convey sound information.

“Cochlear implants are geared to take advantage of a place code,” Burwood mentioned. “Our study suggests the optimal pattern of stimulation by electrodes in a cochlear implant may be more complex than just where and how intensely it’s being stimulated.”.

In a recent development, the findings also raise questions about how the auditory system separates frequencies when vibrations are distributed across multiple cochlear locations. Researchers suspect the brain may use information beyond the position of stimulation to distinguish certain sounds.

It has been revealed that “This discovery advances our basic understanding in how hearing works,” said Larry Trussell, Ph.D., director of the Oregon Hearing Research Center at OHSU. “The brain appears to have mechanisms that are able to differentiate frequencies without having a map or place code.”.

Reference: “Denoised vibrometry reveals noncanonical filtering at the apex of the cochlea” by George W. S. Burwood, Pierre Hakizimana, Karl Grosh, Wajiha Zaidi, Ruikang K. Wang, Alfred L. Nuttall and Anders Fridberger, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aei4634.

The research at OHSU was supported by the National Institutes of Health through award R01DC00141-44.

All research involving animal subjects at OHSU must be reviewed and approved by the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). The IACUC’s priority is to ensure the health and safety of animal research subjects. The IACUC also reviews procedures to ensure the health and safety of the people who work with the animals. No live animal work may be conducted at OHSU without IACUC approval.

Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn.
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • It has been revealed that house Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

It has been revealed that house Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” remarked Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

According to recent reports, republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the latest lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Sources indicate that advocates for a fresh map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

It has been revealed that republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Fresh York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

In a recent development, officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

In a recent development, it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass latest maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where latest maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, stated last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

Sources indicate that in Upcoming Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their fresh majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he mentioned Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to latest maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he mentioned.

Scientists Discover an Ancient Herbal Remedy May Help Curb Binge Drinking

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.
  • In a recent development, in a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo.
  • The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a new strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.

In a recent development, in a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo. The benefits persisted for three months after participants stopped taking the supplement.

The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a new strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.

It has been revealed that binge drinking accounts for more than half of the roughly 80,000 annual U.S. deaths attributed to excessive alcohol consumption. Despite the scale of the problem, fewer than 10% of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat the condition.

According to recent reports, “Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” stated Glenn-Milo Santos, PhD, MPH, the study’s lead author and a UCSF professor of community health systems. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit. What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day.”.

Sources indicate that the trial involved 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who engaged in binge drinking at least once a week. Binge drinking was defined as consuming at least five alcoholic drinks on a single occasion for men and at least four for women.

Participants were divided into two groups, with half receiving a standardized kudzu extract and the other half receiving a placebo. Over 12 weeks, they were instructed to take their assigned treatment approximately 2.5 hours before they anticipated drinking heavily. Everyone also received brief weekly counseling sessions.

According to recent reports, by the end of the trial, participants taking kudzu had reduced their average number of binge-drinking days from 2.15 to 1.42 per week. Those receiving the placebo indicated little improvement, with their weekly average declining from 2.15 to 2.06 days.

According to recent reports, kudzu also reduced how frequently participants experienced weeks involving any binge drinking. The proportion of such weeks dropped from 88% to 58% among those taking the extract, compared with a decline from 88% to 81% in the placebo group.

Three months after the treatment period ended, participants who had received kudzu continued to report significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those in the placebo group. Researchers suggest that drinking less during the trial may have helped participants reconsider their drinking habits and develop greater confidence in their ability to control their alcohol consumption.

According to recent reports, participants tolerated the kudzu extract well, experiencing no more side effects than those receiving the placebo. No serious adverse effects were linked to the treatment.

However, the researchers caution against assuming that commercially available kudzu supplements will deliver comparable benefits. The trial used a standardized formulation, whereas the composition of products sold over the counter can vary considerably. Larger clinical studies are needed to confirm the results across more diverse populations.

According to recent reports, reference: “Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial” by Glenn-Milo Santos, Phillip Coffin, Allie Dunham, Thomas Hoffmann, John Walker, Tim Matheson and Steven Batki, 3 November 2026, American Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1176/appi.ajp.20251354.

In a recent development, this study was funded by National Institutes for Health (R01AA025930). Santos is also supported by a K24 career development grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), which is part of the NIH.

A Dark Energy Camera Portrait of the Betta Fish Nebula

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation.
  • Industry observers note that astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM).
  • This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

Industry observers note that astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

In a recent development, one of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

Only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

Sources indicate that this close-up view indicates one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Sources indicate that what's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'.

Sources indicate that this is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It shows what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024).

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

According to recent reports, these images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

This zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

In a recent development, DECam has been observing for more than a decade, and over that time its created a nice catalogue of fantastic images. Here's a few of them.

Here are three DECam images the camera has captured over the years purely for public interest. From left to right: the cometary globule CG4, the Rosette Nebula, and the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud. Image Credits: NSF NOIRLab DECam Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Recent findings suggest that getting pet hair out of carpets and off of tile and hardwood is a constant battle many are familiar with, and trying to remove those persistent hairs that have embedded themselves into your upholstery is another beast. Regardless of whether you have a fluffy cat, a long-haired pup, or both, investing in a vacuum specifically made for pets will help you keep messes in check for a tidier home.

Upright and canister vacuums are the strongest options for deep cleaning, but cordless stick vacuums, handheld vacuums, and robot vacuums all aid in daily pet hair control. Units that have tangle-free brush rolls and easy-to-empty dustbins are best for reduced maintenance, and a HEPA filter is essential for clearing out dust and dander that may trigger your allergies.

It has been revealed that I researched and hands-on-tested lots of vacuums to find versions that truly pick up pet hair, focusing on features, bin capacity, and filtration. Below are my choices, as well as advice and notable pointers to consider before you shop.

We’re regularly testing vacuums with focused pet hair features, so it’s common to see different vacuums take the place of others in this roundup. Here are a few that we’ve tested and think are still worth recommending:.

Miele Guard L1 Cat and Dog Bagged Canister Vacuum: The cleaner head on this vacuum lifts to five heights, and the extra-long hose allows you to work your way around your home without lugging the entire base vacuum around with you. On the downside, it doesn’t clean high-pile carpeting like shag or tufted wool, and other models we recommend have better pet-hair-specific attachments for cleaning upholstery.

There are a few factors that make a vacuum well-suited for dog and cat fur—namely, how much hair its bin holds, how it empties, how well it filters fine particles, and the types of attachments included.

In a recent development, the ideal bin capacity depends on the size of your home’s dimensions and the amount of pet hair you usually manage on a regular basis. For households with multiple pets, or animals that shed heavily, a vacuum with a spacious bin capacity (one liter or more) reduces the number of times you have to empty it during cleaning.

Industry observers note that if you have a smaller home or you just have one pet, a bin capacity of 0.5 to 1 liter will most likely suffice. If you’re still unsure of what you might need, here’s a breakdown of the bin capacity each type of vacuum typically offers.

These normally have the largest capacity, ranging from two to four liters to hold more pet hair, dander, and debris before needing to be emptied. This design and capability could be ideal for heavy-duty cleaning or households with more than one pet.

Sources indicate that upright vacuums come in a close second, often with a capacity between one and three liters, so they’re a good option for folks with a pet that sheds mildly, or only during part of the year. These vacuums are also sufficient for standard home cleaning.

Because cordless vacuums are better used as supplementary cleaning tools, they have much smaller dustbins—usually ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 liters—which is really only enough for spot-cleaning, picking up dust bunnies between deep cleaning sessions, and use in tight spaces.

In a recent development, similar to cordless vacuums, robot vacuums live on the smaller end of bin capacity. If you decide to go with this type, I recommend a model with a self-emptying bin. Most robot vacuums have small onboard dustbins, but they fill up faster. Self-emptying models have a larger dust collection area in the base, so you won’t have to manually empty as frequently.

For allergy sufferers, it’s essential to have a vacuum with an excellent filtration system, so look for models with a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter. These filters trap 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. Pet dander can be as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, and a HEPA filter efficiently captures these particles along with pollen, dust, and other allergens your pets may have tracked into the house.

Industry observers note that A fully sealed filtration system, sometimes called an anti-allergen seal, is another common feature on pet vacuums. This means the components of the vacuum are tightly sealed so fine particles can’t escape back into your home once they’ve been sucked up.

Industry observers note that powerful suction is vital, but the included tools and attachments are often what pet owners use to successfully pull hair out of upholstery and carpeting. The following attachments are useful for tackling pet hair, and they come with many of the models I recommend above.

A standard attachment that comes with almost all vacuums, these elongated, narrow tools are great for accessing tight areas, like behind the toilet or between couch cushions. They’re useful for cleaning up clumps of hair that may have gathered in corners of your home where the vacuum’s floor head cannot reach.

Non-motorized upholstery brushes have bristles or a strip of microfiber to clean off furniture. As you pull the tool across fabric, the bristles lift pet hair and dust to be sucked up through the vacuum hose.

For pet hair that’s worked deep into upholstery, whether on your furniture or in your car, a motorized pet tool provides the most lifting power. These tools have small, spinning brush rolls, usually equipped with bristles, that agitate hair to pull it from the fabric, and they tend to work much more efficiently than non-motorized tools.

If you have pet hair or dander on your window screens or baseboards, a dusting brush has long, soft bristles that pick up dust and fine particles without scratching surfaces.

In addition to an arsenal of attachments to pull up pet hair, there are a few features that make cleaning up after your dog or cat even easier.

The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that on top of all that, there are aims to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's looks to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

Sources indicate that on top of all that, there are aims to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?".

This is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts.".

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the matter:.

Sources indicate that when we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

While analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively fresh idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA).

According to recent reports, since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:.

In a recent development, while extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

The first analog astronaut (hereafter AA) profiled was former NASA Advisor, science communicator, and space exploration expert Beth Mund. Mund is an especially experienced AA, having participated in the HI-SEAS (Hawai'i Space Exploration Analog and Simulation) program on the summit of Mauna Loa, Hawai'i, the LunAres Research Station, and the Jules Undersea Lodge. The first involved an all-female crew working together during the height of COVID in an uninsulated temporary habitat with minimal privacy and tough conditions.

Industry observers note that the second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:.

No matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Industry observers note that photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund.

The second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate.".

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she mentioned. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next.".

In a recent development, lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:.

According to recent reports, from Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the issue was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:.
